body.objective: Students will be able to identify instruments by sound.
body.iCan: I can identify instruments by sound.
successCriteria: I can identify instruments by their sound
I can name the instrument families
I can describe timbre using descriptive words
body.hook: Close your eyes. A flute and a violin can play the exact same note, yet you can tell them apart instantly. That special colour of a sound is called timbre, and it's how you recognize every instrument and voice.

vocabulary.definition: The unique colour or quality of a sound.
A group of instruments that make sound in a similar way.
Instruments that make sound with vibrating strings, such as violin and guitar.
Instruments played by blowing across or through a reed or mouthpiece, such as flute and clarinet.
Instruments played by buzzing the lips into a mouthpiece, such as trumpet and tuba.
Instruments played by striking, shaking or scraping, such as drums and xylophone.

study.title: Name That Sound
study.question: How can I identify instruments by their sound?
study.passage:
Listening guide (written for this lesson):
Families: Strings (violin, viola, cello, double bass, guitar, harp); Woodwinds (flute, clarinet, oboe, bassoon, saxophone); Brass (trumpet, French horn, trombone, tuba); Percussion (drums, cymbals, xylophone, timpani); Keyboards (piano, organ); Voice.
Instruments from many cultures: koto (Japanese zither), sitar (Indian string instrument), djembe (West African drum), oud (Middle Eastern lute), erhu (Chinese two-string fiddle), Indigenous hand drum.
Timbre words: bright, dark, warm, brassy, breathy, nasal, mellow, buzzy, sharp, smooth.
Activities: 1. Listen to 12 short clips and name the instrument and family. 2. Describe each with two timbre words. 3. Listen to Benjamin Britten's The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra (1946) and raise a card for each family as it plays.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers play clips from public educational recordings.

body.objective: Students will be able to describe music using elements.
body.iCan: I can describe music using elements.
successCriteria: I can describe music using tempo, dynamics, texture and timbre
I can use music vocabulary in my descriptions
I can explain how elements create mood
body.hook: Saying "I like it" about music isn't wrong, but it isn't very useful either. Musicians describe music with a toolkit of elements: tempo, dynamics, texture and timbre. With these words, you can explain exactly what you hear.

vocabulary.definition: How loud or soft the music is.
How many layers of sound there are and how they fit together.
A texture with a single melody line.
A texture with a melody and accompanying chords.
A texture with several independent melodies at once.

study.title: Talk Like a Musician
study.question: How can I describe music using its elements?
study.passage:
Elements toolkit (written for this lesson):
Tempo: slow (largo, adagio), walking pace (andante), fast (allegro, presto); getting faster (accelerando), slower (ritardando).
Dynamics: very soft (pp, pianissimo), soft (p, piano), medium (mf), loud (f, forte), very loud (ff, fortissimo); getting louder (crescendo), softer (decrescendo).
Texture: thin (one or two parts) to thick (many parts); monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic.
Timbre: instruments and tone colours.
Listening task: For three contrasting excerpts, complete the toolkit chart, then write a three-sentence description that ends with the mood. Examples: Edvard Grieg, "In the Hall of the Mountain King" (1875) (accelerando and crescendo); a Gregorian chant (monophonic); a pop ballad (homophonic).
Sentence frame: "The tempo is ___ and the dynamics ___. The texture is ___ with ___ instruments. Together these create a ___ mood."
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers play excerpts from public recordings.
steps: Learn the four elements and their terms

body.objective: Students will be able to compare music from two cultures.
body.iCan: I can compare music from two cultures.
successCriteria: I can compare music from two cultures using musical elements
I can describe the role of music in a culture
I can listen to and talk about music respectfully
body.hook: Inuit throat singing, Cree powwow drumming, Celtic fiddling from Cape Breton, Japanese taiko and Mexican mariachi can all be heard in Canada today. Comparing music from different cultures shows how people everywhere use the same elements in their own ways.

vocabulary.definition: The shared beliefs, customs and arts of a group.
Inuit throat singing, often a game between two women facing each other.
A gathering of many First Nations that includes singing, drumming and dance.
Folk music played on the violin, important in Métis, Acadian and Cape Breton traditions.
Listening with an open mind and learning a music's meaning from its own community.

study.title: Music Across Cultures
study.question: How do music traditions compare, and what do they mean to their communities?
study.passage:
Listening examples (summaries written for this lesson; teachers play clips from community or public educational sources):
A. Inuit katajjaq: two singers face each other and trade quick rhythmic sounds made with breath and throat; traditionally a game, the first to laugh or run out of breath loses. Tanya Tagaq is a well-known Inuk artist who has brought throat singing to new audiences.
B. Powwow drum songs: a group of singers sits around a large drum, singing high, strong vocals in a call-and-response pattern; songs support dancers and gatherings.
C. Métis fiddle music, such as the "Red River Jig": fast, lively fiddle tunes with foot-tapping, played for dancing.
D. Japanese taiko drumming: powerful, coordinated drumming with movement and shouts.
Task: Choose two examples. Compare them with a Venn diagram using tempo, dynamics, texture, timbre and purpose (game, ceremony, dance, celebration). Then write a short comparison.
study.source: Summaries written for this lesson; some songs are ceremonial, so classes listen to examples shared publicly for education.
steps: Note elements and purpose for each
discussion: How is purpose different between two traditions?
What elements did your two examples share?
Why should we learn about music from the people who make it?
study.product: Write a paragraph comparing two music traditions using at least three musical elements and their purpose.
